strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: purely sequential retrieval in deep research agents causes latency and workflow incoherence; the paper identifies a real and timely gap (training models to distinguish parallelizable vs. sequential subqueries).

Automatic dataset construction pipeline (HDS-QA) built from Natural Questions and Google's People Also Ask avoids human annotation, with sensible verification steps (ensuring neither parallel-hop nor hybrid-hop questions are answerable in a single retrieval step).

Consistent empirical gains across five diverse benchmarks, with a particularly large margin on FanOutQA (+15.9 F1) and BrowseComp-50 (+11.5 F1), which are the benchmarks most aligned with the parallel-search motivation.

Thoughtful efficiency analysis: the test-time search scaling experiments under constrained budgets (max turns / max API calls), the AUC efficiency metric, the evidence-coverage analysis (Table 3, Figure 5), and the generated-token budget analysis (Figure 8) go beyond simple end-state accuracy and directly support the paper's efficiency and scalability claims.

Baselines are reasonably comprehensive, spanning non-iterative, iterative single-query, and iterative multi-query methods (Search-o1, Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, RAG-R1), and qualitative case studies illustrate failure modes of sequential baselines.
weaknesses: Potential backbone confound: the proposed model fine-tunes Qwen3-8B, while the strongest trained baselines (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, RAG-R1) use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Part of the reported gains may stem from the stronger base model rather than HDS-QA training. No experiment fine-tunes a baseline recipe on the same backbone, which weakens causal attribution; the evidence-coverage analysis partially mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

Training data is small and narrow: 1,987 synthetic questions derived from NQ-style single-hop seeds via People Also Ask, yielding only 2,111 trajectories. Distribution mismatch with BrowseComp/MedBrowseComp-style tasks is plausible, and there are no ablations on data scale, on the number of parallel hops, or on trajectory filtering thresholds.

BrowseComp-50 is a non-standard, biased subset (the first 50 questions solvable by o3 within five minutes) of only 50 items; combined with the small FanOutQA dev set (310) and no statistical significance testing, several headline claims rest on small, idiosyncratic evaluation sets.

Novelty over concurrent work is thinly argued: RAG-R1 and ParallelSearch (Tan et al. 2025; Zhao et al. 2025) already perform simultaneous multi-query generation/RL training; the paper's main differentiator is the explicit parallel-vs-sequential decomposition in the dataset, but no controlled comparison isolates the benefit of this decomposition over simply training with multi-query data.

Latency is proxied only by 'number of search turns'; the paper does not measure wall-clock latency or discuss whether parallel queries are actually executed concurrently, so the central 'reduces inference latency' claim is only indirectly supported. Similarly, per-query document summarization via Qwen3-32B adds an API call per query, complicating the cost story.

Dataset quality is validated only automatically; no human verification that generated hybrid-hop questions are well-formed, unambiguous, or truly require the intended parallel structure, raising concerns about noisy supervision.

Supervised fine-tuning only on successful trajectories (self-generated by Qwen3-32B, ~27% success rate) may inherit the teacher's search habits; no comparison against RL or preference-based training on the same data, which the authors themselves list as future work.
Reproducibility concerns: dependence on live web search (Jina AI) and time-varying retrieval results; no stated plan for releasing the dataset, code, or trajectories.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: purely sequential querying in agentic RAG causes latency and incoherent workflows; training a model to distinguish parallelizable from sequential subqueries is a sensible and timely angle.

Automatic dataset construction pipeline (HDS-QA) built from Natural Questions with People-Also-Ask expansion and verification that neither parallel-hop nor final questions are answerable in a single retrieval step, removing reliance on human annotation.

Consistent empirical gains across five benchmarks (best F1/MBE on all of them, notably +15.9 F1 on FanOutQA), with evidence-coverage analysis (Table 3, Figure 5) that partially attributes gains to parallel query decomposition rather than backbone differences.

Unusual and useful evaluation of test-time scaling under explicit budget constraints (search turns M_T and API calls M_C), plus generated-token budget analysis in the appendix, going beyond single-point comparisons.
Reasonable breadth of baselines spanning non-iterative, iterative single-query (Search-o1, Search-R1, R1-Searcher), and iterative multi-query (DeepResearcher, RAG-R1) methods.
weaknesses: Limited novelty and positioning: the core idea of emitting multiple parallel queries per turn is already present in DeepResearcher, RAG-R1, and concurrent work (ParallelSearch, Zhao et al. 2025), which the paper acknowledges; the delta is mostly the dataset construction, and the paper does not demonstrate a decisive advantage over these concurrent approaches.

Small training corpus: only 1,987 questions and 2,111 trajectories (27% trajectory success rate), raising questions about whether the gains generalize; no dataset-size ablation or scaling study is provided.

Missing critical ablations: there is no control baseline fine-tuned on an equal number of generic agentic search trajectories (e.g., HotpotQA-derived traces), so it is impossible to tell whether improvements come from explicit parallel/sequential supervision or simply from any well-formed SFT traces on a strong Qwen3-8B backbone.

Backbone mismatch and training-recipe confound: HybridDeepSearcher is Qwen3-8B SFT while GRPO baselines use Qwen2.5-7B; the claim that gains stem from parallelization (Figure 5) is indirect. No RL comparison (e.g., GRPO on HDS-QA) is attempted.

Evaluation validity concerns: F1 is described as 'accuracy'; MBE is model-based scoring with Qwen3-32B, potentially favoring outputs stylistically similar to the teacher; BrowseComp-50 is a non-standard 50-question subset selected by o3 solvability, which introduces selection bias toward easier/retrievable questions; no statistical significance tests or variance estimates anywhere.

Baselines are allowed 10 unconstrained turns while the proposed method's scaling analysis applies budget forcing only to itself; fairness of the AUC and scaling comparisons would be clearer if baselines were evaluated under identical budget constraints in the main results.

Training-data bias risk: trajectories are retained only when the final answer is correct, which may teach shortcuts (e.g., echoing confident retrievals) rather than robust hybrid search behavior; no failure-case or contamination analysis (retrieval of training-like content at test time) is reported.
Reproducibility: no mention of code or dataset release; reliance on proprietary/API services (Google People Also Ask, Jina search, Qwen3-32B summarization) makes exact replication difficult.

Presentation issues: several grammatical errors ('Previous methods exposes'), the motivating Figure 1 example is cherry-picked, and qualitative case studies in the appendix are anecdotal rather than systematic error analysis.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: explicitly training LRMs to distinguish parallelizable from sequential queries addresses a real inefficiency (latency and context growth) in current deep-research agents, and the paper is well positioned against concurrent work (ParallelSearch, RAG-R1).

Automatic dataset construction pipeline (HDS-QA) from Natural Questions + Google People-Also-Ask removes reliance on human annotation, and includes verification steps to ensure both parallel and sequential hops are genuinely required; synthetic trajectories are filtered for correctness.

Comprehensive evaluation across five benchmarks spanning sequential (MuSiQue) and fan-out/exhaustive (FanOutQA, BrowseComp) settings, with multiple metrics (F1, MBE, #Turn, AUC) and a novel accuracy-latency trade-off analysis.

Test-time scaling experiments under both latency (turns) and search-cost (API call) budgets, plus token-budget analysis and an evidence-coverage analysis, provide convincing evidence that the model effectively utilizes larger budgets while baselines plateau.

Consistent gains over strong baselines on the fan-out style benchmarks (+15.9 F1 on FanOutQA, +11.5 F1 on BrowseComp-50), and qualitative case studies clearly illustrate the failure modes of sequential baselines.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: the strongest baselines (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, RAG-R1) use Qwen2.5-7B backbones while HybridDeepSearcher uses the newer, stronger Qwen3-8B; this confounds attribution of gains to the training data vs. the backbone.

Wall-clock latency is never measured; '# Turn' is used as a latency proxy, but each turn can issue many parallel queries and additionally incurs a Qwen3-32B summarization API call per query for our method (Search-o1/DeepResearcher also do, but cost accounting ignores this), so the 'reduced inference latency' claim is only partially supported.

BrowseComp-50 is a small, idiosyncratically selected subset (first 50 questions o3 answers correctly in 5 minutes), raising selection-bias and statistical-significance concerns; on 50 questions the +11.5 F1 gain corresponds to only a handful of items, and no variance or significance testing is reported anywhere.

The training set is very small (1,987 questions, 2,111 trajectories) and single-seed/single-run fine-tuning; there are no ablations on dataset size, number of trajectory samples, filtering thresholds, or sensitivity of results to the SFT-only recipe (no comparison to RL alternatives on the same data).

HDS-QA questions are entity-centric riddle-style questions built from single-entity Wikipedia characteristics; generalization of the hybrid-parallel decomposition skill to other query types (temporal, numeric aggregation, cross-source) is assumed but not analyzed.

Some results are less favorable than the abstract suggests (e.g., RAG-R1 slightly outperforms ours on MuSiQue/FRAMES at low turn budgets, and ours lags under low API-call budgets on MuSiQue/FRAMES), which the text acknowledges only softly; conclusions could be stated more precisely.
Dataset construction depends on Google's People Also Ask feature, which may limit reproducibility and diversity of the question distribution.

strengths: The paper identifies and clearly frames an important, previously underexplored problem: existing search agents (both sequential single-query and parallel multi-query) fail to exhibit genuine test-time search scaling, and provides empirical evidence (Figure 1, Figure 3) supporting this observation.

HDS-QA is a novel and useful contribution: the first dataset explicitly designed for broad (>2 sub-query) parallel search combined with structured aggregation within sequential reasoning, with an automatic pipeline, trajectory filtering by answer correctness, and statistics on parallel width and sequential depth diversity (Appendix B).

Evaluation is unusually thorough: five diverse benchmarks, three categories of baselines, a backbone-matched comparison (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct retrained on HDS-QA), model-scale ablations (4B/8B/32B), a summarizer ablation, a controlled single-query ablation isolating hybrid search behavior, and a GRPO experiment showing RL adds accuracy but reduces efficiency.

Multiple resource-controlled analyses (turn budgets, call budgets, token budgets, evidence coverage rate, performance vs. number of gold evidence documents) directly support the central claim of test-time search scaling rather than relying on a single headline metric.

Qualitative case studies (Appendix F) illustrate concrete failure modes of baselines (incorrect parallelization of dependent queries, duplicate queries, premature termination), adding interpretability to the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: HDS-QA is built from a fixed structural template (one parallel hop + one sequential hop) applied to seed NQ questions via Google People-Also-Ask, raising concerns about diversity, distributional narrowness, and potential mismatch with open-ended benchmarks like BrowseComp; the paper argues diversity emerges in trajectories but the question distribution itself is limited.

The dataset is small (only ~773 questions with at least one correct trajectory out of 1,987; 2,111 trajectories total), and the question-generation pass@4 of 38.9% is modest, so supervision quality/coverage could be a bottleneck; no human validation of generated questions is reported.

Evaluation depends heavily on LLM-as-a-judge (Qwen3-32B) which is the same model family as the trajectory generator, introducing potential judging bias; some inconsistencies (e.g., the 7B variant beating the 8B model on MedBrowseComp, marginal gaps on MedBrowseComp vs RAG-R1) are not analyzed.

BrowseComp† is a custom 150-question subset selected by o3 solvability within 5 minutes, which may bias the benchmark toward easier questions and complicates comparison with prior BrowseComp results; the fairness of comparing budget-constrained 'Ours' against baselines with 10 turns and unlimited calls is only partially mitigated.

Cost accounting is incomplete: our method relies on a Qwen3-32B summarizer API call per query plus web search calls; latency/cost of the summarizer relative to baselines that do not use one is not fully controlled in the efficiency claims, though the summarizer ablation helps.

Novelty is incremental relative to concurrent work (RAG-R1, ParallelSearch, DeepResearcher, task-decomposition methods like ReDel/ADaPT): the core idea of mixing parallel query expansion with sequential reasoning is a natural combination, and the main contribution rests on the dataset and the empirical scaling findings rather than a new method or algorithm.

Claims that 'GRPO may not provide the most effective signal for search scaling' are drawn from a single small-scale GRPO run (20 steps) with a 4B judge for reward; this is under-powered to support general conclusions about RL for search scaling.

strengths: The paper clearly identifies and motivates a real problem: existing search agents do not exhibit consistent test-time search scaling, and the framing of 'parallel breadth vs. sequential depth' is intuitive and well illustrated (Figure 1, the John Carpenter example).

The evaluation is relatively comprehensive: five benchmarks spanning sequential (MuSiQue) and fan-out/parallel (FanOutQA) settings, efficiency metrics (# Turn, a defined AUC metric), evidence coverage analysis, and scaling curves over both turns and API calls.

The ablations are a strong point: a controlled single-query variant trained on the same questions isolates the effect of hybrid search behavior, a GRPO comparison on top of the SFT model, model-scale experiments (4B/8B/32B), and a summarizer ablation (8B vs. 32B vs. none).

The main results are large and consistent: state-of-the-art across all benchmarks with substantial margins on fan-out-heavy tasks, and the training cost (SFT only, ~30 minutes on 8 A100s) is modest, which is practically appealing.
The observation that supervised hybrid-search trajectories outperform GRPO-trained baselines on search scaling is an interesting and potentially influential finding for the sub-area.
weaknesses: Limited novelty of the core method: the contribution reduces to supervised fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories distilled from Qwen3-32B. Concurrent works (RAG-R1, ParallelSearch) already train multi-query parallel search, and task-decomposition/synthesis is well explored (ReDel, ADaPT, Plan*RAG); the claim of 'first dataset' supporting >2 parallel sub-queries feels overstated.

The HDS-QA question template is structurally minimal (one parallel hop + one sequential hop) and built from NQ seeds via Google People-Also-Ask, yielding heavily Wikipedia-centric questions. This raises concerns about (i) distribution mismatch with harder benchmarks like BrowseComp†, (ii) potential train-eval topical overlap with Wikipedia-based benchmarks (MuSiQue, FanOutQA, FRAMES), and (iii) whether the large gains partly reflect stylistic familiarity rather than genuine hybrid search capability. No contamination analysis is provided.

The training set is small and heavily filtered: 1,987 questions with only 38.9% pass@4, retaining 2,111 trajectories. Only 773 questions contribute supervision, and trajectories that 'contain incorrect steps but recover' are kept by design — this is claimed to be valuable but is not ablated, and SFT on erroneous intermediate steps could teach poor patterns.

Baseline fairness concerns: RL baselines (Search-R1, R1-Searcher, DeepResearcher, RAG-R1) use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct while the headline model uses Qwen3-8B with thinking mode; prompt-based baselines (Naive, RAG, Search-o1) are weaker and differently configured. The Qwen2.5-7B re-training helps, but data budgets differ substantially across baselines.

The BrowseComp† subset is custom-curated via o3 solvability (150 questions), which is non-standard, potentially easier/biased, and makes the reported +9.2 F1 gain hard to compare against prior work on full BrowseComp.
Evaluation relies on an LLM judge (Qwen3-32B) and word-level F1, with single runs and no variance or significance testing; the AUC metric, while reasonable, is custom and complicates comparability.

Several unresolved methodological questions remain: the ablation in Table 4 shows the single-query variant falling below Search-o1 in some cases, which complicates the interpretation of where gains come from; GRPO yields accuracy gains but lower AUC, and no alternative reward shaping is explored despite this being flagged as future work.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem statement: the paper provides empirical evidence (Figure 1) that existing search agents fail to exhibit genuine test-time search scaling, and identifies the complementary failure modes of sequential-only (information bottleneck) and parallel-only (synthesis difficulty) approaches.

The proposed hybrid search strategy (parallel query expansion + explicit aggregation before deeper sequential reasoning) is intuitive, well-motivated with concrete examples, and the HDS-QA dataset construction pipeline is described in enough detail (including full prompts in Appendix E) to be reproducible.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse benchmarks (MuSiQue, FanOutQA, FRAMES, MedBrowseComp, BrowseComp†), covering both sequential and fan-out style QA.

The paper addresses fairness concerns proactively: it trains Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (the same backbone as most baselines) on HDS-QA, showing that supervised fine-tuning alone surpasses GRPO-trained baselines, which strengthens the central claim that the hybrid behavior is learnable from supervision.

Thoughtful ablations and analyses: a controlled single-query ablation (Table 4) that isolates the contribution of hybrid search behavior from mere fine-tuning, a GRPO-on-top comparison, model-scale experiments (4B/8B/32B), summarizer ablation, evidence coverage analysis, and robustness analysis grouped by the number of gold evidence documents.

The test-time scaling analysis along two axes (search turns and search API calls), plus an AUC metric capturing the accuracy-latency trade-off, directly supports the headline claim that the model scales monotonically while baselines plateau.
weaknesses: Potential train/eval contamination and knowledge leakage: HDS-QA is seeded from Natural Questions and built via Google 'People Also Ask', so generated questions revolve around popular entities whose answers the teacher (Qwen3-32B) likely already knows. The paper does not report any contamination/overlap analysis with the Wikipedia-based evaluation benchmarks (MuSiQue, FRAMES, FanOutQA), nor check whether fine-tuning data overlaps benchmark questions.

The question generation template is structurally minimal (one parallel hop plus one sequential hop). Although Appendix B reports trajectory diversity, the dataset may not cover the breadth of hybrid search patterns needed to fully support claims of broad generalizability, and the pass@4 of only 38.9% (773/1,987 questions retained) suggests the supervision signal is limited to what the teacher can already solve.

Missing comparisons with the strongest concurrent long-horizon search methods: works such as Gao et al. (2025, 'Beyond ten turns') and WebExplorer are cited but not empirically compared, weakening the 'state-of-the-art' claim; comparisons are restricted to relatively small GRPO-trained 7B baselines.

Some evaluation protocol concerns: BrowseComp† is a custom 150-question subset curated by filtering on o3's 5-minute solvability, which is non-standard and makes absolute numbers hard to contextualize; accuracy relies on LLM-as-a-judge (Qwen3-32B), which may be biased toward the authors' model outputs; and the external summarizer (Qwen3-32B) is applied to only some methods (Search-o1, DeepResearcher, and theirs) but not the RL baselines, creating uneven retrieval conditions.

The budget-controlled scaling comparison in Figure 1/5 is partially asymmetric: their model is forced to answer when budgets are exhausted while baselines run up to 10 turns with unlimited calls, so cross-method scaling comparisons require careful interpretation.

Several reported inconsistencies go unexplained, e.g., F1 (44.1) vs. Acc (20.0) on FanOutQA, and F1 (15.1) exceeding Acc (13.3) on BrowseComp†, leaving uncertainty about answer-format effects on metric validity.
No explicit statement regarding release of the HDS-QA dataset, trajectories, or code, which limits reproducibility of a contribution whose dataset is a central claim.
